title: Compliance Penetration Testing in 2026: SOC 2, PCI, HIPAA
summary: What SOC 2, PCI DSS 4.0.1, HIPAA and ISO 27001 require from a pentest in 2026: cadence, retests, report evidence, and which vendors deliver it.
body_markdown:
PCI DSS is the only one of the four frameworks that names penetration testing outright: Requirement 11.4 calls for internal and external tests at least every 12 months and after significant change. SOC 2 and ISO 27001 do not require a pentest by name, but auditors and enterprise customers expect one as evidence, and HIPAA's current rule asks for periodic technical evaluation, with an annual pentest only in a proposed rule. ## Does SOC 2 Require Penetration Testing?


[SOC 2](https://docs.codeant.ai/compliance/SOC-2) does not list penetration testing as a hard requirement. The Trust Services Criteria are outcome-based, so they describe the security controls you must demonstrate rather than the exact test you must run.


In practice, a penetration test is how you demonstrate them. It is the standard evidence auditors expect for the criteria around vulnerability detection and monitoring, most directly CC7.1, so a documented annual pentest is effectively the norm for a SOC 2 Type II report.


What the auditor cares about is proof. A report that shows exploitable findings were identified, then remediated and retested, maps cleanly to the criteria in a way a raw scanner output does not.


## What Does PCI DSS 4.0.1 Requirement 11.4 Ask for?


PCI DSS is the one framework that names penetration testing directly. Requirement 11.4 of[PCI DSS 4.0.1](https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/) requires both internal and external testing on a documented methodology.


The cadence is explicit. Testing is required at least once every 12 months and after any significant change, with segmentation testing every 12 months for all entities and every six months for service providers. Requirement 11.4.4 also requires retesting to confirm that identified issues were corrected.


One nuance matters for tooling. PCI DSS expects validated, exploitable findings, so a scanner report that lists potential issues without proving them does not satisfy 11.4. That is a direct argument for testing that produces a working proof of exploit.


## Does HIPAA Require a Penetration Test in 2026?


HIPAA is the least prescriptive of the three, for now. The current Security Rule requires a periodic technical evaluation under[164.308(a)(8)](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/index.html) , and a penetration test is the accepted way to meet it.


That is changing. HHS published a proposed rule in December 2024 that would require penetration testing at least once every 12 months and vulnerability scanning every six months, along with stronger controls like MFA and encryption.


The important caveat is status. As of mid-2026 that rule remains proposed, not final, so write to the current evaluation standard today and treat the annual-pentest mandate as likely rather than in force.


For a more detailed look at the testing expectations specific to healthcare organizations, see our guide to[HIPAA penetration testing requirements](https://codeant.ai/blogs/hipaa-penetration-testing-requirements) .

## What Do Auditors Check in a Pentest Report?


Passing an audit is less about running a pentest and more about the evidence it produces. Across all three frameworks, the report should contain the same core elements.


-


A documented, repeatable methodology


-


Each finding mapped to the specific control it satisfies


-


CVSS scoring and risk ranking


-


Proof of exploitation, a working proof of concept, for every finding


-


A retest confirming the fix held


The theme is proof over theory. A report that proves a vulnerability was exploitable, then proves the fix closed it, is worth far more to an assessor than a scanner dump of unconfirmed alerts. This is the same reason[outcome-based testing](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/the-penetration-test-you-only-pay-for-when-it-finds-something) exists, since it is built around confirmed, exploitable findings rather than volume.


> The testing approach also needs to reflect the industry and data being protected. For an industry-specific example, see our guide to[penetration testing for insurance companies](https://codeant.ai/blogs/penetration-testing-for-insurance-companies) .


## Does Continuous Testing Satisfy SOC 2 and PCI DSS the Same Way an Annual Pentest Does?


The annual pentest was designed for a slow release cycle. That assumption breaks for teams shipping weekly, and PCI DSS already reflects it by requiring retesting after any significant change.


If you ship frequently, a once-a-year test cannot keep your evidence current, and triggering a full manual engagement after every release is neither fast nor affordable.[Continuous testing](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/continuous-vs-annual-pentesting) closes that gap by validating changes as they ship and keeping a live audit trail.


That trail is the payoff for compliance. Instead of scrambling to produce evidence before an audit, you have a continuous record of findings, fixes, and retests that maps to your controls year-round. The[penetration testing process](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/penetration-testing-process) is the same, but the cadence matches how you actually build.

## Will My Auditor Accept an AI Pentest Report?


Auditors do not prescribe a method. For SOC 2 and ISO 27001 they check that an independent party tested the system, the scope and dates, the evidence behind each finding, the severity method, and proof that fixes were retested. PCI DSS adds a documented methodology and a qualified, organizationally independent tester (11.4.1 to 11.4.3). Ask any vendor, AI or human, for a sample report and check those points before you buy. CodeAnt's sample report is at[codeant.ai/pentest-sample-report](https://codeant.ai/pentest-sample-report) .


## Does ISO 27001 Require a Penetration Test?


No control in ISO/IEC 27001:2022 says "penetration test". Annex A 8.8 asks you to get information about technical vulnerabilities, evaluate your exposure and act on it, and 8.29 asks for security testing during development and acceptance. A yearly pentest, plus a retest after fixes, is the most common evidence auditors see for both. More detail:[iso-27001-penetration-testing.](https://codeant.ai/blogs/iso-27001-penetration-testing)

## Which Pentest Do I Need for My Audit?


The three frameworks land in different places, but the direction is the same. PCI DSS requires penetration testing outright, SOC 2 expects it as evidence, and HIPAA is on track to mandate it, so if you handle regulated data, an annual pentest is the floor, not the ceiling.


What every auditor rewards is proof. Findings that are validated, mapped to a control, and confirmed fixed on retest are what turn a test into a passed audit, and continuous testing keeps that evidence current instead of stale.
